reference_traces.rationale: Reviewer reports identify the integrated clinical-isolate, genetic, transcriptomic, oxidative-stress, DNA-damage, and metabolic analyses as the contribution; the final paper documents the corresponding mechanistic framework.
Reviewer reports specifically connect enhanced ROS formation and oxidative cellular damage to the observed phenotype; the final paper provides the final experimental description and assay evidence.

Reviewer reports characterize the work as extending prior observations by connecting KatG deficiency with several mechanistic routes to BDQ susceptibility; the final paper presents that multi-mechanism contribution.

Reviewer 2 identified overlap between the initial susceptibility section and prior work. The final discussion acknowledges related preceding observations while framing the present work as a mechanistic investigation, leaving the novelty limit material.

The revised paper explains random selection and adds clinical-strain data, but its final evidence still uses a small validation set and reports one biological replicate for most clinical strains; the clinical-effect and statistical concerns therefore remain partly unresolved.

The response added a discussion of lineage-associated resistance mutations, but the final paper explicitly states that non-KatG resistance and lineage-specific mechanisms were not directly studied. The causal generalization across clinical INH-resistant populations remains partial.

The response clarifies that BacTiter-Glo and OD600 report different endpoints and narrows the transcription-factor claim. The final discussion nevertheless states that not all induced programs sensitized cells and treats the multicomponent mechanism as speculative, so individual causal contributions remain partly resolved.
The reviewer asked whether lineage-specific INH-resistance mechanisms alter BDQ susceptibility. The final paper discusses the issue but states that those effects remain to be investigated.

The response offers saturation as a possible explanation for the lack of additional TMP–SMX sensitivity. The final paper retains this as a possibility and reports discordant MDR versus non-MDR antifolate results, leaving the mechanism unresolved.
Figure-reference inaccuracies were reported in round 1 and stated to have been corrected in the response; this is retained solely as a resolved audit item.
The requested katG complementation experiment was added and the final paper reports complementation-based evidence; this is retained solely as a resolved audit item.
Concerns about the use of “synergy” were addressed by revising the terminology; this is retained solely as a resolved audit item.

limiting_points.suggested_action: Explicit delimitation of the mechanistic advance beyond prior susceptibility observations.
limiting_points.text: The first clinical-susceptibility section has a novelty limit because related observations were already reported; the distinct contribution is the proposed mechanistic basis rather than the existence of the association alone.

supporting_points.text: The contribution links clinical BDQ susceptibility with catalase deficiency through multiple experimentally examined physiological mechanisms, including ROS, DNA damage, transcriptional remodeling, and folate metabolism.

questions.text: How consistently does the BDQ-susceptibility association hold across inhA-associated resistance, katG variants, and Mtb lineages?

questions.suggested_action: Direct testing of the proposed antifolate mechanism in MDR clinical strains.
questions.text: What mechanism explains the absence of additional TMP–SMX sensitization and the lack of TMP/SMX sensitization in MDR clinical strains despite the proposed folate-biosynthesis vulnerability?

strengths.text: The study combines population-scale clinical-isolate observations with targeted genetic and systems-level experiments to examine why catalase-deficient, drug-resistant Mtb can be more susceptible to BDQ.
Orthogonal measurements of ROS-associated oxidative damage connect increased CellROX signal with protein carbonylation and deoxyguanosine oxidation in the catalase-deficient background.

summary.text: The review identifies a mechanistic study of BDQ hyper-susceptibility in drug-resistant Mtb that integrates clinical-isolate patterns with catalase-deficiency models, oxidative-stress and DNA-damage measurements, transcriptional analyses, and folate-pathway experiments. The final paper supports a multi-factor explanation while retaining uncertainty about generalization across clinical resistance genotypes and the contribution of individual mechanisms.

weaknesses.suggested_action: Larger, independently replicated clinical-isolate validation with explicit outcome statistics.
weaknesses.text: The clinical validation remains limited by the small TDR-TB comparison set and by single biological replicates for most clinical strains; the final paper also describes the population-level MIC shift as modest and its clinical impact as unclear.

weaknesses.suggested_action: Direct testing across non-KatG resistance mechanisms and lineages.
weaknesses.text: The central causal framing is narrower than the broad INH-resistant/MDR clinical interpretation: the final paper focuses on catalase-deficiency models and acknowledges that inhA-associated resistance and lineage-specific physiology were not directly resolved.

weaknesses.suggested_action: Quantitative separation of the contributions from individual transcriptional and metabolic changes.
weaknesses.text: The transcriptional mechanism remains associative. ATP-production and growth assays give non-identical results, and the final discussion notes that not all induced transcriptional programs increase BDQ sensitivity, supporting a multicomponent but incompletely resolved explanation.

revision_ledger.residual_summary: Figure-reference errors were reported as corrected; no retained final-state point.
katG complementation was added and documented; no retained final-state point.
Terminology concerning synergy was revised; no retained final-state point.
